opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think a lot of the conversation about AI coding focuses on whether these agents can replace professional software engineers building production systems, and that's honestly not where I've found most of the value in my own work.

A huge amount of the code I need, as a researcher and frankly just as a person who's curious about things, is throwaway code. It's a quick script to scrape some data and see if a hypothesis holds up. It's a little interactive visualization to help me understand a concept, or to explain it to students. It's a one-off tool that does something very specific to my workflow that no commercial product would ever bother to build. The bar for that kind of code is completely different. It doesn't need to be maintainable, it doesn't need to handle every edge case, it doesn't need to be secure against attackers. It just needs to work well enough, right now, for me.

And that's exactly where the weaknesses of these agents matter least. The things people rightly worry about, like subtle bugs, poor architecture, technical debt piling up, or code nobody on the team understands, are mostly problems of software that has to live a long time and be relied upon by others. If I'm going to look at the output, check whether it makes sense, and then throw the code away, a lot of those risks just evaporate.

What it changes is the cost-benefit calculation. Before, there were lots of little ideas I'd have, "it'd be nice to check this" or "I wish I had a tool for that," and I'd never do them because it would take an afternoon of fiddling. Now it takes ten minutes, so I actually do them. That's a qualitative shift in what's worth attempting, and I think it's underappreciated because it doesn't show up in productivity statistics about professional developers.

I'd add one caveat, though. You still need enough judgment to know whether the output is right. For exploratory analysis especially, it's very easy to get a plausible-looking chart that's actually wrong, and if you're drawing conclusions from it, that matters. So "doesn't need to be production quality" isn't the same as "doesn't need to be correct." But within those bounds, I think this is one of the most genuinely useful things the technology does today.

r001.rationale: It describes throwaway scripts used to see whether a research hypothesis holds up.

r002.rationale: It says one-off tools and small ideas become worth pursuing because agents cut the effort from an afternoon to ten minutes.

r003.rationale: It explains that risks such as subtle bugs matter less in code that will be checked and discarded, while clarifying that exploratory results still need to be correct.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: So a lot of the code I write, and I think this is true for a lot of researchers, is code that only needs to run once. It's an analysis script, it's a scraper for a particular dataset, it's a quick simulation to check an intuition before I bother writing it up properly. Nobody else is ever going to read it, it doesn't need tests, it doesn't need to be maintained. It just needs to produce the answer and then I'm done with it.

And for that category, the usual objections to AI-generated code mostly don't apply. People worry, reasonably, that the code is subtly buggy or that it's not the architecture you'd want in a codebase that has to live for five years. But if I'm going to run this once and throw it away, I don't care about the architecture. What I care about is whether the output is right, and that I can usually check directly, because I know what the answer should roughly look like, or I can spot-check a few cases by hand.

The other thing is that for a lot of these tasks, the bottleneck was never the thinking. It was the friction. Remembering the exact matplotlib incantation, figuring out which library parses this weird file format, writing the boilerplate to loop over a directory. That friction was high enough that I'd often just not do the experiment. So the agent doesn't make me a faster programmer so much as it lowers the threshold for which curiosities are worth pursuing. I end up asking questions I wouldn't have asked before, because the cost of getting a quick answer went from an afternoon to ten minutes.

I'd contrast that with production software, where I think the picture is much more mixed. There, the costs of a mistake are borne over a long time, by other people, and the hard part is understanding the system rather than typing. But I'd guess a large fraction of all code ever written is actually this disposable kind, and that's where the value is clearest to me right now.

r001.rationale: It identifies one-off research code, including quick simulations to test an intuition, as a case where AI coding agents are valuable.

r002.rationale: It says agents reduce the friction and time needed to run quick experiments, making curiosities worth pursuing that previously might have been skipped.

r003.rationale: It says common concerns about bugs mostly do not apply to disposable code, but still stresses that the output must be right and can be checked. It does not clearly state that bugs themselves are acceptable.

astra-6.text:
A lot of the value of code is in what it lets you figure out, rather than in the software itself. Maybe I want to analyze a dataset, make a visualization, or test an idea. I might run that code once, get the answer, and throw it away.

For those tasks, a coding agent can dramatically lower the cost of getting started. I don’t need to invest in making the code maintainable or building something that other people can use. I can go from a question to an experiment much more quickly.

Of course, disposable code can still give you the wrong answer. So I still need to check whether the analysis makes sense and whether the code actually does what I intended. But that’s a much narrower responsibility than making software reliable enough to deploy and maintain. And there are a lot of useful things you can do within that space.

r001.rationale: It describes using a coding agent to analyze data, make a visualization, or test an idea with code that may be run once and discarded.

r002.rationale: It says a coding agent lowers the cost of getting started, making one-off tasks quicker without investing in maintainability or broader usability.

r003.rationale: It says disposable code can produce wrong answers and still needs checking. It does not say bugs are acceptable; it only contrasts checking the result with the broader reliability needed for production software.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of the code I want is useful once. I might want to analyze a dataset, make a visualization, or build a little tool to explore an idea. The result matters, but the code itself doesn’t necessarily need to be maintained for years.

That changes the tradeoff. With production software, getting something that appears to work is only the beginning. You also have to think about reliability, security, and how someone will understand and modify it later. For a small, temporary task, I can often check the output directly and get the value without taking on all of those obligations.

So coding agents make it practical to do things that wouldn’t otherwise justify the time. I can try an idea, see whether it’s useful, and throw the code away when I’m done. I still have to verify the result, but that can be much easier than writing the whole program myself.

r001.rationale: It describes one-use code for analyzing data or exploring an idea and says coding agents make such tasks practical, conveying the value of testing an idea with disposable code.

r002.rationale: It says coding agents make small tasks worthwhile when they would not otherwise justify the time, explaining that they reduce the effort of creating the code.

r003.rationale: It says temporary code can be checked directly without taking on production obligations, but does not state that bugs can be acceptable.
